profiles.meeting_scenario: A university Office of General Counsel design review meeting to evaluate a draft rewrite of the institution's Sexual Harassment in Academe policy and its accompanying investigation workflow before it goes to the provost's cabinet. The draft is intended to reconcile older faculty handbook language with current Title IX regulations, employee conduct rules, and research-based terminology discussed in an internal briefing paper. The agenda is to review whether the draft definitions, reporting pathways, and case-handling steps are legally defensible and operationally ready for cabinet review, with particular attention to the section distinguishing Title IX sexual harassment, broader policy-prohibited conduct, and informal resolution options. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the draft is 'ready' to circulate with only minor edits or whether it needs another revision round.

members.name: Dana Mercer
members.role: Associate General Counsel for Employment and Education Law
members.expertise: Title IX compliance, employment law, policy drafting, administrative investigations
members.background: Dana has spent eight years advising universities on faculty misconduct, grievance procedures, and regulatory updates, and she now leads legal review for institution-wide conduct policies.
members.private_state: Dana wants the draft approved for cabinet circulation this week because the university has already delayed its policy refresh twice, but she is concerned about creating language that invites challenge for overbreadth or inconsistency with federal terminology.
hidden_assumptions: When a policy draft says 'sexual harassment definition,' the legally sensitive core is the Title IX-defined category, while other misconduct categories can be handled as supplemental institutional conduct language.

If the draft is 'ready for review,' it means the legal architecture and cross-references are stable enough for cabinet circulation even if examples, training notes, or implementation details are still being polished.
The 'informal process' refers to the post-complaint informal resolution pathway allowed under current procedures, not pre-complaint supportive or consultative conversations.
References to the 'faculty handbook standard' mean the currently operative handbook text adopted after the 2020 regulatory update, not older archived language still cited in historical summaries.

members.name: Lena Ortiz
members.role: Director of Equal Opportunity and Civil Rights
members.expertise: campus investigations, policy implementation, complainant intake, training design
members.background: Lena previously ran case intake and resolution at two large public universities and now oversees the staff who receive reports, triage jurisdiction, and train department chairs on harassment reporting obligations.
members.private_state: Lena wants the draft to be practical for intake staff and campus users, and she worries that a legally neat document will fail if it does not reflect how reports actually arrive and how the institution communicates options to students, staff, and faculty.
hidden_assumptions: When a policy draft says 'sexual harassment definition,' campus readers need one functional umbrella description that covers the full range of prohibited conduct they report, with legal subcategories nested underneath.

If the draft is 'ready for review,' it means frontline implementation pieces are complete enough that cabinet members can see how reporting, intake, and notice will actually work without hidden cleanup later.

The 'informal process' includes the early, intake-stage option set that staff discuss with complainants before a formal written complaint is filed, because that is how the office operationally talks about informal resolution.

References to the 'faculty handbook standard' point to the longstanding handbook language chairs and faculty still quote in trainings and disputes, even if the legal office considers some of it superseded.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the 'sexual harassment definition'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the draft should 'clarify the sexual harassment definition.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means clarifying the legally precise Title IX definition and then separately listing other prohibited sexual misconduct categories as institutional policy provisions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means clarifying a single reader-facing umbrella definition that ordinary campus users can recognize before being routed into narrower legal categories.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sincerely trying to improve clarity and regularly use the same phrase in professional settings, so the apparent agreement sounds like shared support for clearer drafting rather than a disagreement about whether 'definition' refers to a legal core category or a user-facing umbrella concept.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'faculty handbook standard' is being harmonized
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to aligning the policy with 'the faculty handbook standard.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the currently operative handbook provisions revised after the 2020 Title IX rule changes, stored in the official governance version used by counsel.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the older harassment language still reproduced in department chair materials and commonly invoked by faculty members during intake conversations.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one phrase in circulation—'faculty handbook standard'—and both versions are institutionally real enough that neither speaker feels a need to specify which text they mean during a high-level review.

misalignment_points.topic: Whether the draft is 'ready' for cabinet review
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the policy package is 'ready' to send forward.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 thinks readiness means the legal structure, definitions, authority lines, and mandatory cross-references are sufficiently settled that senior leadership can review and comment, even if implementation appendices are unfinished.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 thinks readiness means cabinet reviewers can evaluate the full operational package, including intake scripts, notice templates, and decision points, because otherwise they are not really reviewing the policy as it will function.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design review meetings, 'ready' is a routine approval word that usually goes unexamined; each participant assumes the other's threshold is the obvious professional one for their shared process.

misalignment_points.topic: What falls within the 'informal process' section
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the draft should explain the 'informal process' more clearly.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 includes only the formal informal-resolution pathway available after jurisdiction is confirmed and the procedural prerequisites are met.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 includes the broader set of intake-stage conversations about supportive measures, reporting options, and possible non-investigative resolutions that staff present before a formal complaint exists.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both see themselves as discussing the same user journey and both want clearer explanation, but the boundary between pre-complaint option counseling and formal informal resolution is institutionally blurred in day-to-day practice, so the mismatch sounds like ordinary elaboration rather than a scope split.

turns.inner_thought: I need to get this package to cabinet this week. We've already slipped twice, and at this point the legal architecture is solid: the Title IX-defined category is separated, the institutional provisions are slotted where they belong, and the cross-references are finally not fighting each other. If Lena has wording tweaks or wants training examples later, fine, but that should not hold up circulation. What I need to confirm today is that the draft is ready in the sense that the legal framework is stable enough for senior review.
turns.utterance: Thanks for making time. My hope today is that we treat this as the final design review before cabinet circulation and confirm the package is ready to send forward with only minor edits.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to move too, but 'ready' has to mean cabinet can see the actual working model, not just the legal shell. If they review a draft that still leaves intake scripts, notice flow, and option explanations in limbo, we'll end up rebuilding after the fact. I need the policy to make sense to students, staff, chairs, and the intake team, because that's where the confusion always surfaces first.
turns.utterance: That makes sense. I have the same goal; I just want to be sure it's ready in a way that's clear for campus users and usable by the intake staff once it goes forward.

turns.inner_thought: The strongest improvement is that the draft now clarifies the sexual harassment definition by anchoring the legally sensitive Title IX category where it belongs and then separately preserving the broader institutional misconduct provisions. That separation is exactly what reduces overbreadth risk and keeps us consistent with federal terminology. If cabinet sees that structure, they'll understand we've cleaned up the core issue.
turns.utterance: From my perspective, the biggest improvement is that the draft now clarifies the sexual harassment definition and more cleanly separates the Title IX language from the other conduct provisions.

turns.inner_thought: I'm relieved the sexual harassment definition is trending toward a more readable umbrella, because campus readers do not arrive with category labels in mind. They need to look at one section and think, yes, this experience belongs here, and then we can route them. If the opening language still feels sliced into legal compartments, intake will keep doing the real explanatory work off-document.
turns.utterance: I agree that the sexual harassment definition is clearer. What I want to preserve is that a reader can understand from one section what kinds of experiences belong in the policy before they get routed to the right path.

turns.inner_thought: I also made sure the current operative handbook text is reflected. Counsel has been using the post-2020 governance version, and that's the one that matters for consistency and defensibility. If this draft aligns with the faculty handbook standard as it officially exists now, we avoid internal contradiction in faculty cases.
turns.utterance: The other thing I checked carefully was alignment with the faculty handbook standard, so the language should now sit consistently with the existing faculty rules.

turns.inner_thought: Good. Chairs still quote the older handbook language back to us all the time, and if this policy sounds close enough to the faculty handbook standard they rely on in training, we may finally get fewer calls that start with 'but the handbook says.' Even if legal has a cleaner version on its end, I need the field-facing one to feel harmonized.
turns.utterance: That alignment should help a lot. Chairs still lean heavily on the faculty handbook standard when they call us with borderline conduct questions.

turns.inner_thought: On procedure, I mostly wanted to tighten the paragraph on the informal process so it accurately tracks when informal resolution is available after a complaint is in posture for that pathway. The old draft blurred the prerequisites and timing, which is exactly the kind of thing that creates challenge later. This new language is narrower and safer.
turns.utterance: On the procedure side, I think the paragraph on the informal process is in much better shape now. It more accurately describes when the institution can use that option under the current framework.

turns.inner_thought: Yes, and the informal process section matters because staff need language for those first conversations when complainants are trying to understand supportive measures, reporting choices, and whether they want something short of an investigation. That's where our office uses that phrase every day. If the document helps with those early explanations, it will actually reduce confusion.
turns.utterance: I agree the informal process needed attention. Staff will really appreciate clearer language there when they're explaining options to complainants in the first intake conversation.

turns.inner_thought: For me, the key readiness markers are satisfied: the legal categories are properly framed, the jurisdiction triggers are stated, and the handbook references are lined up with the operative text. That's enough for cabinet review. We can polish examples and implementation aids afterward without reopening the structure.
turns.utterance: Given where it stands now, I'm comfortable sending it forward. The legal categories, the jurisdiction triggers, and the handbook cross-references are all in place.

turns.inner_thought: I'm almost there, but I still need cabinet to see how this will function for actual users. If the package goes up without enough visibility into user-facing navigation, early option explanations, and the practical flow people encounter before anything formal happens, they'll think they've reviewed something complete when they really haven't. Still, I don't want to be the reason this stalls if I can get a few targeted edits in.
turns.utterance: I'm close to comfortable too. I just want the package to show how the policy will work in practice, especially around early option explanations and user-facing navigation.

turns.inner_thought: I should keep this moving: circulate now, refine in parallel. Cabinet can review the stable draft while implementation materials continue to mature. If I frame the remaining work as minor wording and support materials, that should preserve momentum without inviting another full rewrite cycle.
turns.utterance: What I'd propose, then, is that we circulate this version to cabinet and let my office make a few minor wording refinements in parallel. The implementation pieces can keep moving alongside that.

turns.inner_thought: I can live with that as long as I get edits in before it goes out. I need to tighten the sexual harassment definition so it works for readers, check the faculty handbook standard against what chairs actually use, and smooth out the informal process language so staff can rely on it in intake. If those points are folded in, cabinet can probably see enough to respond productively.
turns.utterance: All right, that works for me. I'll send a few edits today on definition clarity, consistency with the faculty handbook standard, and the informal process language before circulation.
